extracted.intended_audience: military officers, judge advocates, and legal advisors in the United States Army
extracted.subtask_short: military legal guidance on troop use
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and regulatory standards governing (1) when and how U.S. military forces may be employed in aid of civil authority (including posse comitatus limits, presidential proclamation, use of force, cross‑border rules, disposition of seized property, and treaty occupations) and (2) the statutory restrictions on Army bands competing with civilian musicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unsolicited military intervention in state civil disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commander cannot volunteer to intervene in a case of civil disturbance in violation of State laws; in the absence of the requisite orders he may not even march or array his command for the purpose of exerting a moral effect or an effect in terrorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a demonstration could compromise U.S. authority and insult State sovereignty (cited authorities: R.30, 125, Mar. 1870; 32, 241, Jan. 1872; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal troops remain under Presidential direction (not state governors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A military force employed according to Article IV, section 4, of the Constitution is to remain under the direction and orders of the President as Commander in Chief and his military subordinates; it cannot be placed under the direct orders or exclusive disposition of the governor of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: R.30, 172, March 1870; C.5354, Nov. 19, 1898; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on military service as a posse comitatus for state/local law execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The military forces of the United States cannot, as such, be permitted in any event to serve upon the posse comitatus of a sheriff or other executive official whose function it is to execute the local laws of a State or Territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited: R.36, 450, May 1875; 39, 458, 577, Mar. and June 1878; C.11928, Jan. 21, 1902; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory restriction: Army not lawful as posse comitatus except when authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 of the act of June 18, 1878 provides 'it shall not be lawful to employ any part of the Army of the United States as a posse comitatus... except in such cases and under such circumstances as such employment of said force may be expressly authorized by the Constitution or by act of Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: employment as posse comitatus requires express constitutional or congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to employ Army to secure due service of process
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a marshal or deputy marshal was prevented from making due service of judicial process by forcible resistance of an unlawful assemblage, the President was expressly authorized by section 5298, R.S., to employ such part of the Army as he might deem necessary to secure the due service of such process and execute the laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and command relationships of Philippine Scouts when assisting constabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philippine Scouts are part of the Military Establishment; when ordered to assist the constabulary they remain under strictly military command by officers of the Army, and are employed under the direction of their military superiors while supporting civil agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their employment is appropriate for limited/localized disturbances where constabulary plus one or more companies of scouts can restore order; larger disturbances call for general military employment under the President. (Statutes: sec. 36 act Feb. 2, 1901; act Jan. 30, 1903; cases C.17508 Feb. 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Army ordinarily not responsible for maintenance of civil order except in insurrection or resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers and men of the Regular Army have, under ordinary circumstances, no responsibilities in connection with the maintenance of civil order and no duties in respect to general execution of the laws; they become charged with such responsibility only when insurrection exists or when resistance is encountered in execution of the laws, and then act pursuant to instructions from the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil governor's role and limits in use of military forces in territories
rubrics_metrics.description: In territories (e.g., the Philippine Islands) the civil governor acts on behalf of the President with civil agencies; military forces may be placed at his disposal to be employed under his general direction but under military officers of rank; if disturbance is large, military commander conducts operations under President's general direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of military assistance is determined by conference between civil and military authorities; reference C.17508, Feb. 15, 1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on using troops for tasks like killing animals or other nonessential civil tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Troops should not be placed on duties such as killing wild horses or other noxious animals on forest reserves; doing so would entail endless complications (e.g., property damage claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: C.23846, Sept. 15, 1908 — avoid employing troops on duties that risk civil liability or unnecessary complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential proclamation requirement before using troops in the States
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5300, R.S., charges the President with a duty analogous to the 'reading of the riot act' by sheriff: by issuing a proclamation. Until such proclamation is issued, troops of the United States will not be used to preserve order in any one of the States of the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: When State requests federal aid, federal forces must be directed by Federal authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State has exhausted its coercive resources and has requested Federal protection, the Federal Government must direct its own forces and cannot transfer its own functions to a State; Federal authorities will direct the operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True whether the President commands in person or devolves duty on a subordinate. Case: C.8383, May 26, 1900.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential discretion over size and area of troop deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: The President (or officer entrusted by him) is the judge of the size of the force to send and the area to be occupied; the occupied district may vary from one or two points to extensive portions of the State's territory; measures depend on circumstances and may include instituting martial law if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Troops must not nullify the republican-form guarantee of the State
rubrics_metrics.description: When Federal troops are sent into a State to protect it or guarantee federal statutes, they must do nothing which will nullify the guarantee in the Federal Constitution of a republican form of government to the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to guard infrastructure and protect against cross‑border lawless bands
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sections 5298–5299 R.S. and constitutional power, guarding essential infrastructure (e.g., high bridges, post routes, military roads) and guarding against invasion by lawless bands from across the boundary is within the President's/commander's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality laws apply in peacetime and define 'military expedition' broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutrality laws are enforceable even absent a state of public war; any combination organized and provided with means within U.S. territory to go to a foreign country to make war on a Government with which the U.S. is at peace is a 'military expedition' under the statute — number of men or completeness of organization is not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act of March 4, 1909 (35 Stat. 1090) and cases: C.22132, Apr. 22, 1911.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force to enforce neutrality: force necessary allowed; deadly force only after warning
rubrics_metrics.description: In enforcing section 14 of the act of March 4, 1909 a military detachment may resort to all force that appears necessary, even deadly weapons; the actual use of sabre, bayonet, or firearm will generally be preceded by due warning and used only when no lesser measure may reasonably be expected to accomplish the lawful end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to report credible cross‑border threat intelligence to civil authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When the commanding general adjacent to the boundary has information that bands of armed men are planning to cross the border and make war on a friendly country, he should furnish such information at once to the nearest U.S. marshal or U.S. attorney to permit proper civil action.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to cross into friendly foreign territory in pursuit
rubrics_metrics.description: When enforcing neutrality or preserving U.S. territory, there is no authority for U.S. armed forces to cross the boundary into the territory of a friendly country even to pursue armed forces that have crossed from U.S. territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of contraband/seized property near the border
rubrics_metrics.description: When arms, ammunition, animals, or other contraband are seized by American troops near the border, the commanding general should as soon as possible turn such seized property over to the Federal civil authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when state writ of replevin seeks seized property
rubrics_metrics.description: If a writ of replevin issues out of a State court for property captured by American troops, the commanding officer should resist it, notify the State court the property is held under U.S. authority, and advise the U.S. attorney; if a Federal court writ issues, follow advice of the U.S. attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible diplomatic/messengerial measures to stop cross‑border fire and funding
rubrics_metrics.description: If fire is directed across the border into U.S. territory during a neighboring civil war, the commanding general may employ a civilian to deliver a message to opposing commanders requesting cessation; such messenger may be paid from the 'Contingencies of the Army' appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to defend and aggressively protect troops when deliberately fired upon
rubrics_metrics.description: If insurgents or opposing forces deliberately fire across the border on American troops, the commanding general may defend and act aggressively to the extent necessary to protect his troops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of neutrality enforcement are primarily federal; avoid imposing state costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of executing neutrality laws and protecting U.S. territory in unusual emergencies is primarily a charge against the United States rather than against the State; commanding generals should maintain cordial relations with State authorities but avoid involving States in unusual costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal troops may not be used to support execution of State laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A commanding general of Federal troops is not authorized to support the authorities of a State in the execution of State laws; Federal forces are not to be used in enforcement of State law per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fingerprinting of interned foreign troops entering the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: When troops cross the boundary from a friendly country being subjected to civil war and are interned within the United States, there is no occasion under which the fingerprints of such persons should be taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty/treaty‑protocol occupation duty: sole criterion is maintenance of free communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article IX of the peace protocol (China, 1901), occupation of certain points to maintain open communication between capital and sea authorizes U.S. forces to act (including by force if necessary) to prevent acts that would interrupt such communication; maintaining free communication is the sole criterion guiding the commanding officer's decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition exists only when identical form of musical service is sought and civilian musicians desire to render similar service
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on Army bands competing with local musicians applies when the same form of music is called for and there exists one or more civilian organizations in the locality capable of rendering similar service (even if their quality is inferior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If a brass band is desired and no civil brass band exists in locality, an Army band may lawfully render the service (C.14639, May 14, 1910; June 10 and Oct. 14, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality, price, and union affiliations are not factors in determining competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of local music, the price charged for musical services, and the union affiliations of civil musicians are not material factors in determining whether competition exists between Army bands and civilian musicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: C.14639 (multiple dates) — quality (I.A.3), price (I.A.4), union affiliation (I.A.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition applies to both Army bands and individual members
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of May 11, 1908 (35 Stat. 110) is equally applicable to bands and to individual members thereof; members are restricted similarly to bands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post commander decides if competition exists but cannot judge civilian band merits; burden on requester
rubrics_metrics.description: The post commander is charged with determining whether acceptance of an engagement by an Army band will place it in competition with local musicians, but he has no discretion to pass upon relative merits of civilian bands; those desiring the Army band must establish there are no similar civil organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where 'competition' does not exist (free service, competent orders, instruction, retired list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition does not exist where (1) music by military band is furnished free; (2) the Army band plays for civilians under competent orders; (3) a member serves as instructor to a civil band; (4) bandsmen on the retired list (not being a band) are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations and cases: C.14639 (Sept. 17, 1908; Oct. 31, 1911; others); C.24179 Dec. 9, 1908 re retired list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer bands and procurement: public money/use of instruments restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Public money cannot be used to buy music for bands not authorized by law as part of the military establishment; instruments procurement is restricted to reasonable needs of lawfully authorized bands, though excess stock may be used to promote welfare of enlisted men; volunteer bands composed of enlisted men maintained at posts may fall within the prohibition.
